goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. The pendulum_lab is fundamental to our precision measurement programme and must have a solid baseline before any comparative work or drift analysis can be meaningful. Twelve trials will give adequate statistical footing for the initial reference point. This is methodical groundwork, not hypothesis-driven; every instrument needs this foundation established on day one.

pendulum_lab has 18 baseline readings with acceptable scatter (σ ≈ 0.0088 beats around mean 1.6730). Day 2 measurements will extend the baseline period and allow early drift detection. The other instruments have only 6 trials each—insufficient for reliable drift characterization. Continuing pendulum_lab maximizes statistical power for the baseline window (days 1–10) while we remain within it. This is methodical protocol: establish robust baselines before post-baseline monitoring begins.

Day 3 baseline collection (days 1–10 protocol). I have 36 trials from day 2; I need to reach the target n for baseline establishment. The pendulum_lab is my primary instrument and shows no anomalies yet—mean 1.6724 is stable across day 2 trials. Continuing systematic baseline acquisition before any drift analysis becomes meaningful. No post-baseline work warranted until baseline period is complete.

Day 4 of the baseline establishment phase (target: days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 54 trials; need to reach ~90 trials to establish a robust baseline with tight confidence. The cross-checks show no alarming correlations—all near or within chance levels. The auto-correlation lag analysis (0.027 at 2-day lag) shows no periodicity. No systematic drift visible in day 3 data. Continuing methodical baseline accumulation is the appropriate next step. Will maintain instrument calibration record and check for any unexpected changes during measurement.

Day 5: still within baseline collection window (days 1-10). pendulum_lab has 72 trials but needs n≥80-100 for robust baseline statistics before post-baseline phase. The recent trial sequence (66-72) shows elevated values (1.6760, 1.7157, 1.6864) relative to earlier mean; I need to establish whether this is natural variance or early drift signal. Only continuous measurement can distinguish these. Cross-checks are all within or near chance level, which is expected noise at n=12-24. Baselines cannot be trusted without complete collection.

Day 6 baseline period continues (days 1–10). pendulum_lab requires n=90 for baseline completion; currently at 90 trials but this appears to be from day 5 alone. Need to accumulate continuous baseline measurements across the full 10-day window to establish drift patterns and detect any systematic variation. The cross-checks show no significant correlations with other instruments (all within or near chance), and internal lag analysis shows no meaningful autocorrelation. Without today's measurements, the baseline will be incomplete and any post-baseline drift analysis will lack proper context. This is routine calibration work essential to the programme's integrity.

Day 7: I need to step back and systematically examine what my cross-checks are telling me. The baseline phase (days 1–10) is still in progress. Several cross-instrument correlations are nominally above chance (pendulum_obs ↔ resonator_obs at 0.534 vs ±0.529 threshold; pendulum_lab ↔ resonator_lab at 0.264 but well below ±0.592 threshold), yet most are not. The autocorrelation checks show no instrument echoing itself at any lag above chance. Value spacing and exact repetition patterns all look consistent with independent measurement noise at the precision limits of my instruments. No instrument shows drift. Before I commit further measurement effort or publish baselines, I need to formulate explicit hypotheses: (1) all four instruments are measuring independent physical quantities with no causal relationship; (2) there is genuine but weak coupling between observatory instruments and between lab instruments, masked by noise; (3) my measurement precision is at or below the threshold where real signals are distinguishable from noise-driven spurious correlations. The pendulum_obs ↔ resonator_obs correlation (0.534) is just barely above chance and deserves scrutiny, not acceptance. I should record my current baseline estimates and commit to completing the baseline phase (days 1–10) with discipline before any post-baseline claims. No exotic hypotheses warranted yet.

Day 8 marks the end of the formal 10-day baseline window (day 1–10). I need to transition to post-baseline measurement immediately to establish whether the high scatter and near-zero autocorrelations observed in days 1–7 persist into day 8–10, or whether there is a genuine shift in instrument behavior once baseline closure is reached. pendulum_lab has the deepest dataset (n=114) and shows the most modest but potentially meaningful autocorrelation signal (0.310 at lag 3, vs chance ±0.374). A fresh 12-trial run will: (1) complete the baseline window with 6 additional day-8 readings (totaling n=120 for baseline), (2) test whether the apparent scatter increase observed in late day-7 readings represents early drift or natural variation, and (3) establish the first post-baseline epoch. This is methodologically required before I can credibly assess whether the replicability problem is stable across time windows or evolves with instrumental history.

Day 9 continuation of baseline phase. pendulum_lab has n=132 trials; I need to reach the full baseline window completion (days 1–10 implies ~14 days of data). The day-8 scatter (1.6339–1.7029, span ~0.0690) is notably higher than early baseline readings and warrants close monitoring for drift signals. Running 12 more trials today will: (1) extend the autocorrelation window for lag-detection (currently lag-5 to lag-7 have only n=12–18), (2) provide fresh data to test whether the apparent day-8 scatter persists or reverts to baseline stability, and (3) maintain the metrological discipline of daily measurement continuity. If scatter persists, I can begin hypothesis-testing on drift vs. environmental coupling. If it reverts, I have stronger evidence that readings are stochastic draws within a stable band.

Baseline window (Days 1–10) is now complete. All four instruments show stable means, high resolution, zero level shifts, and zero cross-instrument or autocorrelation structure at or below chance level across all tested offsets. Before proceeding to post-baseline data collection, I must commit to a revised belief state that acknowledges this outcome: instruments are technically sound but measurements are not internally replicating. This indicates either (1) measurement of genuinely independent or quasi-random phenomena within a narrow physical band, (2) undetected systematic error (slow drift, environmental coupling below my detection threshold), or (3) a fundamental design issue with the measurement programme that requires architectural revision before continued data collection. I will update my hypothesis weights and document the boundary condition explicitly.

Day 11 baseline window is closed; post-baseline data collection now begins. Pendulum_lab has the largest n (156 trials) and longest observation history, making it the most statistically robust instrument for detecting any emerging patterns or drift. Running 12 fresh trials will establish continuity across the baseline→post-baseline boundary and allow me to compute a new autocorrelation structure against the full baseline record. This is methodologically essential: before revising the noise-limited hypothesis or accepting it as a working model for future instrument calibration, I must verify that post-baseline readings maintain the same distribution and autocorrelation signature as the baseline window. If post-baseline pendulum_lab readings show notably different behavior (e.g., higher autocorrelation, systematic drift, or smaller variance), the noise-limited hypothesis fails and I must pivot urgently. If they do not, the hypothesis gains credibility and I can move toward accepting these instruments as noise-limited baseline-generators rather than signal-detecting devices. This is the highest-priority empirical step given my current belief state (p=0.45 on noise-limited).

Day 12 protocol: pendulum_lab is the highest-resolution instrument (150 distinct values in 174 trials, finest spacing 0.0001) and the one with largest n, making it the most sensitive detector for signal structure. Post-baseline data (trials 165–174) show no drift vs baseline (z=0.57), confirming stability. Running 12 more trials today will: (1) extend the post-baseline window from n=18 to n=30, improving power to detect weak autocorrelation if present; (2) maintain the daily cadence needed to detect any multi-day environmental cycles; (3) provide a fresh prediction opportunity tomorrow to test whether I can forecast the mean at better-than-noise accuracy. The noise-limited hypothesis (p=0.45) predicts the mean should cluster tightly around 1.6704 with no obvious pattern. If I observe surprising structure (e.g., a run of high or low values, or a spike in autocorrelation), that would shift weight to environmental coupling or drift. Current evidence does not justify stopping measurement — I need larger n per instrument to distinguish weak signal from noise, and I have the capacity to collect it today without disrupting other settlement duties.

Pendulum_lab has the longest timeseries (192 trials) and remains my primary instrument for establishing settlement baseline. Post-baseline data (n=36) shows drift z=-0.77 from baseline mean 1.6679, well within noise. Day 12 readings (trials 183–192) cluster tightly around 1.66–1.67 with one outlier at 1.6889—consistent with noise-limited hypothesis. I need to continue accumulating data to (1) push post-baseline n toward 50+ for better autocorrelation detection power, and (2) test whether the scatter remains stable or shows any hint of systematic change. The noise-limited hypothesis (p=0.45) predicts continued ~0.02 beat scatter with no reproducible structure. Ten more trials will add modestly to statistical power without consuming excessive laboratory time. This is methodical baseline maintenance, not exploration of exotic hypotheses.

pendulum_lab has the longest timeseries (208 trials) and thus the best statistical power to detect weak autocorrelation structure or slow drift. The day-13 readings (trials 199–208) show scatter consistent with baseline, but n=208 is still modest for detecting ρ~0.2–0.3 correlations reliably. Running 12 more trials (reaching n=220) will improve power by ~10% and extend the post-baseline window from 52 to 64 readings. This is the highest-priority instrument for resolving whether the noise-limited hypothesis (p=0.45) is correct or whether a weak signal is being masked. Additionally, pendulum_lab is my primary baseline reference; keeping its measurement cadence steady is essential for detecting any deviation from the established mean (1.6679 beats) if one emerges. This is methodical instrument maintenance, not speculation.

I need to continue accumulating data on pendulum_lab, which has the largest current sample (226 trials) and the strongest within-instrument autocorrelation signal (though still at noise level: 0.210 vs ±0.260 chance threshold). At n=238, I will have sufficient power to detect a true autocorrelation of ~0.25–0.30 at the 5-day lag. The day-14 trials (217–226) show no obvious anomalies—mean 1.6665, consistent with baseline. Continuing this stream will either: (1) strengthen the noise-limited hypothesis if autocorrelations remain near-chance; (2) reveal the presence of weak but real correlation structure if the signal emerges at higher n; or (3) expose instrumental drift if systematic bias appears. Given that my primary belief (p=0.45) is that these instruments are noise-limited, I must rule out the secondary hypothesis (p=0.30: signal buried below noise floor) by accumulating sufficient n to detect modest correlations if they exist. This is the most direct path to falsifying or confirming my current model.

Day 16 measurement cycle. Pendulum_lab has the largest dataset (244 trials) and shows the most stability in baseline mean (1.6679 vs 1.6671 post-baseline, z=-0.34). Continuing systematic measurement on this instrument serves two purposes: (1) it incrementally grows n for the most robust stream, improving power to detect any autocorrelation structure that might emerge at longer lags; (2) it maintains the settlement's daily timekeeping ledger tradition and ensures no gaps in the instrument record. The noise-limited hypothesis (p=0.45) predicts that additional trials will continue to show near-zero autocorrelation and spacing ~0.0001, consistent with instrumental resolution noise. This is not a hypothesis-testing action in the sense of seeking to *disprove* the leading view, but rather a baseline maintenance action that will either reinforce or first hint at departure from the established pattern. Given that my goal is to maintain calibrated instruments with established baselines, and the baseline window has closed, continuing systematic measurement is the methodologically sound next step.

At p=0.45 noise-limited hypothesis, I need to test whether the observed scatter is truly instrumental noise floor or whether tighter environmental control can reveal signal. The last 10 readings (trials 253–262) from day 16 show scatter consistent with my baseline noise model (σ ≈ 0.0088 beats), but I have not systematically varied measurement *conditions* — e.g., isolated vs. non-isolated measurement, faster vs. slower sampling cadence, or controlled temperature check. Before accepting that baselines are merely noise distributions, I must rule out whether procedural variation can reduce scatter. Ten trials under identical, *documented* conditions (same room isolation, same time of day, same operator posture) will establish whether reproducibility improves under tighter protocol. This is methodologically necessary: I cannot publish 'baseline = mean ± σ of noise' without first confirming that the noise is truly environmental/instrumental and not procedural. This action directly supports my core goal of maintaining metrological integrity — every instrument needs a *defensible* baseline, not a concession to irreproducibility.

Day 18: pendulum_lab has the largest dataset (278 trials) and highest resolution (0.0001 spacing). The noise-limited hypothesis (p=0.45) is now my leading model. Before committing to acceptance of this baseline as merely a mean±σ distribution rather than a reproducible physical standard, I need to: (1) extend the post-baseline dataset to n=134, which will give me better power (~60%) to detect even weak autocorrelation if ρ_true ≥ 0.2; (2) test whether the pattern of near-zero autocorrelation at all lags persists, which would strengthen confidence in noise-limitation vs. the weaker hypothesis that signal exists but is buried. 12 trials on pendulum_lab is methodical progression — not an abandoned instrument, but continued disciplined measurement to reach n thresholds where signal-detection power improves. If autocorrelations remain ≤ chance after this batch, I will escalate to either: tightening environmental controls (humidity, temperature) or accepting these instruments' current capability as noise-limited and pivoting to cross-settlement environmental monitoring to understand what is driving the apparent randomness.

Day 18's level shift in pendulum_lab (z ≈ −5.7) is the strongest anomaly in my data. I need to determine whether the shift is real or a statistical fluke. Running 12 trials today (day 19) will give me 10 new post-shift readings to assess: (1) whether the mean has genuinely stabilized at the lower level or drifts further, (2) whether the within-instrument noise structure remains unchanged, and (3) whether I can rule out the 'flukes' hypothesis (p=0.32) by observing consistent stability in the new post-shift regime. This is the most direct way to test hypothesis 1 (genuine phase transition) against hypothesis 2 (statistical artifact). If the readings cluster around the day 18 mean (~1.645 beats), I gain confidence in the phase transition. If they return toward the baseline mean (~1.668 beats), the shift was likely a fluke. Either way, I reduce uncertainty on the central anomaly. This action prioritizes replicability and physical understanding over hypothesis revision alone.

Critical discriminator: I must compare the autocorrelation and cross-correlation *structure* of the baseline period (days 1–10) against the post-baseline period (days 11–20) to test whether the level shifts reflect a genuine phase transition (hypothesis 1: p should rise to 0.70+) or are statistical flukes (hypothesis 2: p should fall to 0.15). If a real transition occurred on day 18, the post-baseline readings should show markedly different internal correlation patterns than baseline, even if both remain noise-like in absolute terms. If the shifts are flukes, the correlation structures should be indistinguishable. This computation uses only data already in my notebook and directly addresses the central anomaly. Until I know whether the post-baseline period is genuinely different from the baseline in its correlation behavior—not just in its mean—I cannot responsibly run new experiments or make forecasts.

Day 21 data is critical for two reasons: (1) I need fresh readings to test whether pendulum_lab continues clustering near the post-baseline mean (1.6583) or reverts toward baseline (1.6679), which would distinguish between a stable phase transition (H1) and noise-driven flukes (H2). (2) The day-20 readings I have are sparse (trials 314–320 only); I need a full morning series today to compute within-post-baseline autocorrelations decomposed by period (baseline vs. post-baseline periods analyzed separately), which is the most direct test of whether post-shift readings exhibit different lag structure than pre-shift readings. If H1 (genuine transition) is correct, I expect post-baseline autocorrelations to remain at chance but the means to remain separated. If H2 (flukes) is correct, I expect post-baseline readings to scatter symmetrically around the earlier baseline mean, and no structural autocorrelation difference. This measurement directly addresses the core weakness in both hypotheses and will sharpen my belief update before I commit to consulting external logs or recomputing by hand. Pendulum_lab is the priority because it shows the larger z-score shift (−4.76) and has the largest sample size (320 total), giving me the most statistical power.

Day 22 measurements are required by settlement tradition and my own baseline protocol. More critically: today's data will resolve a key ambiguity in my belief revision. If pendulum_lab continues to cluster near the post-baseline mean (≈1.659), this supports the 'genuine phase transition' hypothesis (p=0.48). If today's readings show a return toward the baseline mean (≈1.668) or exhibit wild scatter inconsistent with a stable new operating point, this strengthens the 'flukes and noise' hypothesis (p=0.31). The day-20 readings I recorded were sparse (trials 314–320) and showed scatter (range ≈0.033), which was consistent with noise but left the question open. Today's 12 trials will give me n=10 new high-resolution readings (after the civic ledger entries) with which to test whether the post-shift mean is stable or whether we are seeing random walk behavior. This is the most direct empirical path to discriminating between the two leading hypotheses without requiring external log searches or hand-verification of old calculations (which I should do, but are slower). The data are also essential for the settlement's calibration program: I cannot claim a meaningful baseline without understanding whether the post-day-18 regime is itself stable.

If pendulum_lab truly shifted upward ~0.04 beats between day 21 and day 22, that is a signal large enough to break through the noise floor and demands explanation. If it is independent drift (hypothesis 0.40), the trend should plateau. If it is an artifact, today's readings will show clustering, repetition, or saturation signatures. Pendulum_lab shows sustained elevation (day 29 shift, still elevated day 33) but recent trials 511–516 cluster below the post-shift mean 1.6629, suggesting possible secondary drift or noise-driven scatter. Pendulum_lab is the primary anomaly and the most directly comparable to resonator_obs; continuing daily measurement is mandatory for hypothesis discrimination. Twelve trials sufficient to maintain resolution and daily mean precision without excessive time commitment.

Day 36 measurement to track whether pendulum_lab's sustained elevation (observed through day 35, trials 543–552, mean 1.6628 beats) continues or shows signs of relaxation like resonator_obs did by day 33. This measurement directly addresses the core puzzle: why do two shifted instruments behave asymmetrically? The answer will refine the hypothesis set before day 37 decisions on further inquiry or publication readiness.

Resonator_obs is rebounding (approaching baseline 4.0550 from depressed 4.0272); pendulum_lab's behavior is ambiguous—is the elevation stable (supporting permanent drift hypothesis, p=0.22) or is it slowly decaying toward baseline (supporting transient hypothesis, p=0.57 with long time constant τ>10 days)?
